secondShift.eyebrow: {ss}: second shift production at your plant
secondShift.h1: We run your line on a shift your plant doesn’t cover.
secondShift.lead: Your filling line is already paid for. On a shift your plant doesn’t cover, VKC runs it as a service: you buy the shift’s output, finished and documented, not hours of work.

body: A {ss} is a production shift that VKC runs for you. Before it starts, we agree on what it has to produce: the product, the container, the specification and the count. Then we run it, and what comes back to you is finished, packed product and the record of how it was made.
That is why it is priced per unit or per shift. The price follows the output, because the output is what you are buying.
The line stays yours. How the shift runs is ours.

body: Every {ss} is documented on our QC sheets and in our production log. Together they are the written account of the shift: what ran, and how it was checked.
If a question comes up about a lot the next morning, the answer is on paper rather than in someone’s memory.

steps: We walk your line with you and look at the product, the containers and the equipment.
We agree on the output and the price, per unit or per shift.
When the shift comes, our lead hand directs it and our crew runs your line.
The shift is documented on our QC sheets and in our production log, and you get your line back.

contractPackaging.h1: Contract packaging for the overflow your line can’t absorb
contractPackaging.lead: When orders outrun your line, send the overflow to VKC. We fill it, label it, kit it and pack it at our facility, as a co-packer for liquids and pastes.

list: Filling, by weight or to a line on the container, whichever your product calls for.
Labelling.
Kitting: putting separate components together into one package.
Packing, so the product leaves ready to ship.
And [toll blending](/services/toll-blending), if the product has to be made before it is packed.

body: A bottleneck is the slowest step in a plant, the one everything else waits on. It is also the neck of the bottle we fill. {bn} works on both readings: it takes volume away from the step that is holding you back and puts it through our line instead.
These container families have already been through our line. If yours is not listed, tell us what it is.
The first thing we will ask is how thick your product is: water-thin, pourable, thick or paste. It decides how the product is filled, how fast, and which of our fill methods fits.

tollBlending.lead: You own the formula. We make the batch at our facility and, if you need it, fill and pack it there too.

body: Toll blending means we mix your product to your formula and your specification. The formula is yours; the work of making the batch is ours.
The word is an old one: a toll is the fee paid to have your own material processed by someone else. You pay for the processing, and the product stays yours.
It suits a product that sells well enough to need more batches than you want to make yourself, or a new product you want made before you invest in equipment of your own.

{bn} puts blending, filling and packing at the same facility. A batch made here can go into bottles, jugs, pails or kits without another truck ride in between, with one quote and one place to call about it.
Cleaners, lubricants, sealers, coatings and colourants. Each behaves differently in a mixer and in a container; the industry pages say how.

bottlesAndJugs.h1: Bottles and jugs for products that pour
bottlesAndJugs.lead: HDPE bottles and D-jugs carry most cleaners and many lubricants. Here are the ones that have already been through our line, and the two ways we fill them.

sections.h2: Bottles and jugs we have run
body: This list is a record of what we have filled, not a limit on what we will look at. If your bottle isn’t on it, send us its name or a sample.
Weigh-fill puts the same weight of product in every container. It suits a product sold by weight, and a product that foams, where the level is hard to read until the foam settles.
Fill-to-line brings every container to the same visible level. A row of bottles filled to the line looks even on a shelf, which matters when a buyer compares one bottle with the one beside it.
Which one fits is usually the product’s call, not ours. We’ll tell you which one we would use, and why.

A bottle is only finished once it is closed and labelled. So when you ask for a quote, the closure and the label are part of the question: what they are, who supplies them, and whether we are the ones putting them on.

list: The bottle or jug: its name, size and material, or a sample.
The closure it takes, and who supplies it.
The label, if we are applying it.
Whether the product foams, drips or strings when it pours.
Units per run, how often you run, and the date the first run ships.

body: If the product has to be made first, [toll blending](/services/toll-blending) happens in the same building as the fill. If the bottle is sold as part of a set, see [kits](/containers/kits). Heavier fills go in [pails](/containers/pails).

pails.h1: Pails for thick, heavy and industrial products
pails.lead: Plastic pails, metal pails and Ropak containers are where thick products usually go: sealers, coatings, pastes, and lubricants sold by the pail.

body: Plastic, metal and Ropak, in the sizes listed below. If your pail is a different one, send us its name or a sample.
The container is usually chosen before it reaches us: by the product’s chemistry, by what your own customer expects, or by what your line already runs. We fill the one you sell in.
Thick products fill slowly and settle slowly. A paste doesn’t level itself in a pail the way a liquid does, so the surface can mislead anyone reading the fill by eye.
That is where weigh-fill earns its place: the scale reads the same weight whatever the surface looks like.

list: The pail: plastic, metal or Ropak, its size, and its lid.
The product, and how thick it is: pourable, thick or paste.
Whether it is sold by weight or by volume.
The label, if we are applying it.
Units per run, how often you run, and the date the first run ships.

body: A pail often holds a product that was blended for the job. [Toll blending](/services/toll-blending) and filling happen at the same facility, so the batch doesn’t travel between them. Lighter products go in [bottles and jugs](/containers/bottles-and-jugs).

kits.h1: Consumer kits, assembled from your components
kits.lead: A kit is several products sold as one: a bottle and its brush, a sealer and its applicator, a set built for a store shelf. We put the pieces together into one finished package.

body: Kitting means bringing separate components together in one package that sells as a single unit. The components can be filled products, accessories such as a brush or a cloth, and printed pieces such as an instruction sheet.
Consumer kits have already been through our facility. The list stays short on purpose: a kit is defined by what goes into it, and no two are alike.

A kit is hand assembly in a plant built for flow. It needs table space, a count of every component, and time the filling line can’t spare. Seasonal kits and promotional sets add a deadline on top. It is careful work, and a missing component comes back as a return. Sending the assembly out keeps your line on what it does best.

list: One finished kit, or a photo of one, as the reference.
The list of components, and who supplies each one.
The outer package the kit is sold in.
How the pieces sit in the package.
Kits per run, and the date they have to ship.

body: When a kit holds a product that also has to be filled, both jobs can happen at our facility: the [bottle](/containers/bottles-and-jugs) is filled, then goes straight into the kit. One quote, one delivery date, one number to call.
